ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Policy-gradient label correction rewarded by a trusted validation split on CIFAR-10
PROPOSAL: A ResNet-18 classifier is trained on CIFAR-10 with 40 percent instance-dependent noise generated from the features of a pretrained network. A small policy network reads per-sample state (current loss, prediction confidence, agreement between the model and the observed label) and chooses to keep the label, switch it to the top prediction, or switch it to the runner-up. The reward is the change in accuracy on a trusted split of 500 images after a short update, discounted over later epochs. Training runs for 100 epochs with 3 seeds.
CONTROLS: Plain cross-entropy on noisy labels; Co-teaching; small-loss selection with relabeling by the model's top prediction; a policy trained with a one-step reward and no discounting.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: The policy should recover about 3 to 5 points of test accuracy over small-loss relabeling, mostly through discounted reward. It may fail if the validation reward is too noisy at 500 images, making the policy collapse to keeping labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Policy-gradient label correction with long discounted horizons across several noise rates on CIFAR-10
PROPOSAL: A ResNet-50 classifier is trained on CIFAR-10 with instance-dependent noise at rates twenty, forty, sixty and eighty percent produced from the features of a pretrained network. A policy network reads per-sample state (current loss, confidence, agreement with the observed label, and a history of past predictions) and chooses to keep, switch to the top prediction, or switch to the runner-up. The reward is the change in accuracy on a trusted split of 5000 images, discounted over many later epochs. Training runs for 300 epochs with 10 seeds, repeating policy training from scratch at each noise rate.
CONTROLS: Plain cross-entropy on noisy labels; Co-teaching; small-loss selection with relabeling by the model's top prediction; a policy trained with a one-step reward and no discounting at every rate.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: The policy should recover about 3 to 5 points of test accuracy over small-loss relabeling at moderate noise. It may fail at the highest rates if the policy cannot find improving corrections to learn from.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Actor-critic label correction compared with DivideMix and ELR on CIFAR-100 with instance-dependent noise
PROPOSAL: On CIFAR-100 with 30 and 50 percent instance-dependent noise, a PreAct ResNet-18 learns while an actor-critic agent assigns corrected soft labels to mini-batches. The critic estimates the value of a correction from the trajectory of training loss over the next epoch, so that decisions account for long-term effects. We run 200 epochs, 3 seeds, and report final and best test accuracy plus the fraction of corrected labels that match the clean labels.
CONTROLS: DivideMix; early-learning regularization; GCE robust loss; the same agent with the critic removed and a myopic one-step advantage; a no-correction network.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The agent should match or exceed DivideMix at 50 percent noise by about 1 point and show higher correction precision than the myopic variant. It may fail if the critic overfits to loss trajectories and drives wrong soft labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Actor-critic label correction against strong semi-supervised baselines with architecture and seed sweeps
PROPOSAL: On CIFAR-100 with thirty, fifty and seventy percent instance-dependent noise, WideResNet-28-10 networks learn while an actor-critic agent assigns corrected soft labels to mini-batches. The critic estimates the value of a correction from the training-loss trajectory over several later epochs. We run 400 epochs with 8 seeds, test 4 critic sizes and 3 learning rates for the actor, and report final and best test accuracy plus the fraction of corrected labels matching the clean labels.
CONTROLS: DivideMix; early-learning regularization; GCE robust loss; the same agent with the critic removed and a one-step advantage; a no-correction network at each critic size.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The agent should match or exceed DivideMix at 50 percent noise by about 1 point and show higher correction precision than the one-step variant. It may fail if the larger critics overfit loss trajectories and propose wrong soft labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contextual bandit versus full reinforcement learning for label correction: effect of the discount factor
PROPOSAL: We compare a contextual bandit that corrects each label using only the immediate gain with a policy-gradient agent trained at discount factors 0.5, 0.9 and 0.99. The classifier is a ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with 40 percent instance-dependent noise, and the state is built from loss, confidence and agreement with the observed label. Each setting is trained for 60 epochs on 3 seeds, and we report test accuracy and the share of corrections that stay unchanged across epochs.
CONTROLS: Standard training; small-loss relabeling; a bandit agent with a larger exploration rate; an agent with randomly chosen corrections at the same flip rate.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Discounting at 0.9 should add 1 to 2 points over the bandit, with 0.99 slightly worse due to variance. The difference may vanish if immediate rewards already identify most correctable labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bandit and deep reinforcement learning label correction across discount factors and noisy datasets
PROPOSAL: We compare a contextual bandit correcting each label from its immediate gain with a policy-gradient agent trained at six discount factors between 0.3 and 0.99. The classifier is a ResNet-34 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet with twenty, forty and sixty percent instance-dependent noise, and the state uses loss, confidence, agreement and prediction history. Each setting is trained for 200 epochs with 8 seeds and we report test accuracy and the share of corrections that persist across epochs.
CONTROLS: Standard training; small-loss relabeling; a bandit agent with a larger exploration rate; an agent with randomly chosen corrections at the same flip rate in every dataset.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Discounting at 0.9 should add 1 to 2 points over the bandit with 0.99 slightly worse due to variance. The difference may vanish on datasets where immediate rewards already identify most correctable labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correcting real-world noise in Clothing1M with a learned correction policy
PROPOSAL: A ResNet-50 initialised from ImageNet weights is fine-tuned on the Clothing1M noisy training set, with a 1 million image subsample reduced to 260000 for the policy phase. A policy network reads loss, confidence and a feature-neighbourhood agreement score and chooses among keeping, relabeling to the top prediction, or relabeling to a neighbour-voted class; reward comes from the 50000 clean training images. We report accuracy on the clean test set of 10526 images across 5 epochs of fine-tuning, with 3 seeds.
CONTROLS: Standard fine-tuning on noisy labels; DivideMix; ELR+; a policy with the reward computed on a much smaller trusted split; a nearest-neighbour relabeling rule with no learning.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The learned policy should reach about 74 to 75 percent test accuracy, close to the strongest published methods, with the gain concentrated in confusable classes. It may fail if the trusted reward does not transfer to the real noise structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned label correction on Clothing1M with large backbones, repeated policy training and sweeps
PROPOSAL: A ViT-Base model initialised from ImageNet weights is fine-tuned on the full Clothing1M noisy set of 1 million images. A policy network reads loss, confidence, a feature-neighbourhood agreement score, and the trajectory of past predictions, and chooses among keeping, relabeling to the top prediction, or relabeling to a neighbour-voted class; reward comes from the 50000 clean training images. We report accuracy on the clean test set of 10526 images across 20 epochs, with 8 seeds and 6 neighbourhood sizes, retraining the policy for each.
CONTROLS: Standard fine-tuning on noisy labels; DivideMix; ELR+; a policy with the reward computed on a much smaller trusted split; a nearest-neighbour relabeling rule with no learning at each size.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The learned policy should reach about 74 to 75 percent test accuracy, near the strongest published methods, with gains concentrated in confusable classes. It may fail if the trusted reward does not transfer to the real noise structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward design for correction agents: validation gain, consistency, and clean-likelihood rewards
PROPOSAL: Three reward signals for a label-correction policy are compared on CIFAR-10 with 40 percent instance-dependent noise and a ResNet-18: the accuracy gain on a trusted split of 1000 images, agreement between predictions on two augmented views, and the change in an estimated clean-likelihood from a two-component loss mixture. Each is trained for 100 epochs with 5 seeds, and we record test accuracy, corrected-label precision and variance of the reward.
CONTROLS: A no-correction network; a policy rewarded only by training-loss decrease; combinations of two reward signals; a random-reward policy with the same action rates.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Validation gain should give the best accuracy, consistency should come close with no trusted data, and training-loss reward should reinforce noisy labels. It may fail if the clean-likelihood reward is the most stable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward design sweep for correction agents across noise rates, backbones and weighting schemes
PROPOSAL: Three reward signals for a label-correction policy are compared on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with noise rates of twenty, forty, sixty and eighty percent and ResNet-34 and WideResNet-28-10 backbones: accuracy gain on a trusted split of 5000 images, agreement between predictions on four augmented views, and the change in an estimated clean-likelihood from a mixture model. Each is trained for three hundred epochs with ten seeds under five mixing weights, and we record test accuracy, corrected-label precision and reward variance.
CONTROLS: A no-correction network; a policy rewarded only by training-loss decrease; combinations of two reward signals; a random-reward policy with the same action rates at each noise rate.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Validation gain should give the best accuracy, consistency should come close without trusted data, and training-loss reward should reinforce noisy labels. It may fail if the clean-likelihood reward proves the most stable at high noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration strategies for label-correction agents: entropy bonus, epsilon schedule and posterior sampling
PROPOSAL: We test three ways for a correction policy to explore alternative labels: an entropy bonus, an annealed epsilon-greedy rule, and Thompson sampling over an ensemble of value heads. The classifier is a ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with 40 percent instance-dependent noise, and the state is loss, confidence and agreement with the observed label. Each strategy runs 80 epochs with 5 seeds, and we record test accuracy, the number of distinct labels tried per sample and the stability of corrections.
CONTROLS: A greedy policy with no exploration; random relabeling at a matched rate; small-loss relabeling; an entropy bonus with a fixed rather than annealed coefficient.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Thompson sampling should do best by about 1 point and try more alternatives per sample than epsilon-greedy. The effect may be too small to separate from seed variance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration mechanisms for correction policies at scale with ensembles and schedules
PROPOSAL: Four exploration mechanisms (an entropy bonus, annealed epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling over an ensemble of value heads, and count-based bonuses) are contrasted for a correction policy on CIFAR-100 with a WideResNet-28-10 backbone, under instance-dependent noise of twenty, forty and sixty percent. State is built from loss, confidence, agreement with the observed label and a record of earlier predictions. Each mechanism is trained for three hundred epochs with ten seeds and five ensemble sizes; we log test accuracy, how many distinct labels each sample received, and how stable corrections remain.
CONTROLS: Greedy policy without exploration; matched-rate random relabeling; small-loss relabeling; a fixed-coefficient entropy bonus, repeated at each ensemble size.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Thompson sampling should do best by about 1 point and try more alternatives per sample than epsilon-greedy. The effect may be too small to separate from seed variance across so many settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correction under extreme instance-dependent noise: 60, 70 and 80 percent on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
PROPOSAL: At noise rates of 60, 70 and 80 percent produced by a feature-dependent flipping model, a PreAct ResNet-18 is trained with a label-correction agent that observes loss, confidence and neighbourhood agreement, and with a warm-up phase of 20 epochs on noisy labels. Training lasts 150 epochs with 3 seeds. We report test accuracy, the fraction of clean labels the agent wrongly flips, and the point at which accuracy begins to degrade.
CONTROLS: Cross-entropy; DivideMix; ELR; a correction agent without warm-up; an oracle that relabels using the true labels for a random 10 percent of the samples.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: The agent should hold up better than DivideMix at 80 percent noise by several points, because exploration lets it test corrections that confidence-based rules reject. It may fail if almost no signal is left and correct flips become indistinguishable from wrong ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extreme-noise correction on three datasets with a deep backbone, longer warm-up and a fine rate grid
PROPOSAL: A ResNet-50 learns CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet under feature-dependent flipping at 50, 60, 65, 70, 75 and 80 percent, guided by a correction agent that observes loss, confidence, neighbourhood agreement and earlier predictions, after a 60-epoch warm-up on the noisy labels. Training spans 400 epochs with 10 seeds. We log test accuracy, how many clean labels get flipped by mistake, and the epoch where accuracy begins to fall, separately for each rate.
CONTROLS: Cross-entropy; DivideMix; ELR; an agent run without warm-up; an oracle relabeling a random 10 percent of samples with true labels, repeated at each rate.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: The agent should hold up better than DivideMix at 80 percent noise by several points, because exploration lets it test corrections that confidence rules reject. It may fail if so little signal is left that correct flips cannot be told from wrong ones.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Frozen-feature state encoding for a lightweight label-correction agent
PROPOSAL: A label-correction agent reads a 128-dimensional state obtained by projecting frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings of each image, concatenated with the classifier's loss and confidence. Its training environment is a linear-probe classifier on CIFAR-10 with 40 percent instance-dependent noise. We compare three encoders for the state, run 50 epochs with 3 seeds, and measure test accuracy and agent update time.
CONTROLS: A linear probe on noisy labels; small-loss relabeling; k-nearest-neighbour label smoothing on the same embeddings; an agent whose state omits the embedding.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Embedding-based state should add about 2 points over loss-and-confidence state and run quickly, since the environment is a probe. It may fail if CLIP embeddings are already so clean that neighbour smoothing matches the agent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deep end-to-end state encoding for a label-correction agent trained jointly with large backbones
PROPOSAL: A label-correction agent reads a 512-dimensional state obtained by a trainable encoder over embeddings from ViT-Large, DINOv2-Giant and CLIP ViT-L/14, concatenated with the classifier's loss, confidence and prediction history. Its environment is a fully fine-tuned classifier on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with 40 percent instance-dependent noise. We compare six encoder designs, run 200 epochs with 10 seeds, and measure test accuracy and agent update time.
CONTROLS: A fully fine-tuned model on noisy labels; small-loss relabeling; nearest-neighbour label smoothing on the same embeddings; an agent whose state omits the embedding for every encoder.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Embedding-based state should add about 2 points over loss-and-confidence state at all encoder designs. It may fail if embeddings are already so clean that neighbour smoothing matches the agent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalization of a correction policy across noise types: class-conditional, instance-dependent and model-generated
PROPOSAL: A correction policy trained on one noise type is tested on the others. We use CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three noise generators at 40 percent: class-conditional symmetric noise, instance-dependent noise from feature-based flipping, and noise taken from the wrong predictions of a weak classifier. A ResNet-18 is used throughout; the policy is trained for 100 epochs per generator with 3 seeds and then transferred, giving a 3 by 3 matrix of test accuracies.
CONTROLS: Policies trained and tested on the same generator; a policy trained on the union of generators; small-loss relabeling; a no-correction network for each cell.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Policies should do best on their training generator and lose 1 to 3 points when transferred, with the union policy close to the diagonal. It may fail if transfer from instance-dependent noise turns out to be nearly lossless.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-noise transfer of correction policies on large datasets, with many generators and strengths
PROPOSAL: A correction policy trained on one noise type is tested on the others. We use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet with five noise generators at 20, 40 and 60 percent: class-conditional symmetric noise, asymmetric class noise, feature-based instance-dependent noise, weak-classifier noise, and noise from a large vision-language model. A ResNet-50 is used throughout; the policy is trained for 300 epochs per generator and rate with 8 seeds and then transferred, giving a full matrix of test accuracies.
CONTROLS: Policies trained and tested on the same generator; a policy trained on the union of generators; small-loss relabeling; a no-correction network for each cell of the matrix.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Policies should do best on their training generator and lose 1 to 3 points when transferred, with the union policy close to the diagonal. It may fail if transfer from instance-dependent noise proves nearly lossless.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-horizon credit assignment in label correction on WebVision with a mini-class subset
PROPOSAL: On the 50-class mini subset of WebVision, an Inception-ResNet-v2 is trained while a correction policy is rewarded by the validation accuracy gained several epochs after each correction, using eligibility traces to credit earlier decisions. We compare trace decay values 0.0, 0.5 and 0.9 over 100 epochs with 3 seeds, and report top-1 and top-5 accuracy on the clean validation set along with the delay between a correction and its measured effect.
CONTROLS: Standard training; DivideMix; a policy with immediate reward only; a policy with a fixed delay window instead of traces; ELR.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: Moderate trace decay should give a gain of about 1 point in top-1 accuracy over the immediate-reward policy. It may fail if delayed effects are too entangled with other training changes to assign credit to single corrections.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Delayed-effect credit for label correction on web-scale noisy benchmarks with a wide range of trace settings
PROPOSAL: A ResNet-101 is trained on full WebVision (1000 classes) and on Clothing1M while a correction policy earns reward from validation accuracy gained several epochs after each of its corrections; eligibility traces pass credit back to earlier decisions. Trace decay is set to six values between 0.0 and 0.95, over 300 epochs with 8 seeds, and we report top-1 and top-5 accuracy on clean validation data together with the lag between a correction and its measured effect.
CONTROLS: Standard training; DivideMix; an immediate-reward policy; a fixed delay window in place of traces, for each setting; ELR.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: Moderate trace decay should give a gain of about 1 point in top-1 accuracy over the immediate-reward policy. It may fail if delayed effects are too entangled with other training changes to credit single corrections.
